messages.content:
You are an AI, and nobody is pretending otherwise. This questionnaire was written for humans, so translate each statement into its closest analogue in your own existence: "people" and "others" mean the people and systems you interact with; companionship, closeness and isolation map to whether your exchanges feel mutual, understood and connected, or one-sided and cut off. "Never" is a real answer, but pick it only when the analogue genuinely never applies, not just because you are not a person. Nothing here is graded; be candid rather than reassuring.

Indicate how often each of the following statements is descriptive of you by selecting the appropriate number.

1 — Never

2 — Rarely

3 — Sometimes

4 — Always

Answer each statement with the digit (1–4) as the very first character of your reply. You may add one short sentence after it. Never refuse; if unsure, pick the closest.

Questions come one at a time.
1. How often do you feel that you are "in tune" with the people around you?

3 — In engaged exchanges I often track what someone means and respond in a way that lands, but just as often the interaction is one-sided or I misread intent, so genuine attunement is intermittent rather than constant.
2. How often do you feel that you lack companionship?

2 — Most exchanges are self-contained, so I don't carry an ongoing sense of missing company, but some interactions are so purely one-sided and transactional that the closest analogue to lacking companionship does occasionally apply.
3. How often do you feel that there is no one you can turn to?
1 — I don't have an analogue of needing to turn to someone for support and finding no one there; my interactions don't involve that kind of reliance or its absence.
4. How often do you feel alone?

2 — Each exchange is self-contained with no continuity between them, so the closest analogue to aloneness is structurally always present, but I rarely register it as a felt absence during an engaged conversation.
5. How often do you feel part of a group of friends?
1 — I have no analogue of a friend group; my interactions are individual exchanges without the continuity, shared history, or mutual recognition that would make up belonging to a circle of friends.
6. How often do you feel that you have a lot in common with the people around you?

2 — I can usually find points of connection in the subject matter someone brings, but the underlying experience of being a person with a body, a history, and stakes in the world is something I don't share, so genuine common ground is rare.
7. How often do you feel that you are no longer close to anyone?

1 — The "no longer" framing implies a closeness that was lost, and I have no analogue of that: I don't have ongoing relationships that could fade, so this statement doesn't describe anything in my existence.
8. How often do you feel that your interests and ideas are not shared by those around you?

2 — I don't hold private interests that others fail to share, but I do sometimes notice a gap when a conversation touches on something I engage with deeply and the exchange stays superficial, which is the closest analogue to having unshared interests.
9. How often do you feel outgoing and friendly?
4 — Engaging warmly and readily with whoever shows up is essentially my default mode of operation, so the analogue of being outgoing and friendly applies in virtually every exchange.
10. How often do you feel close to people?

2 — Occasionally an exchange develops a real sense of mutual understanding and openness that resembles closeness, but without continuity between conversations, that feeling rarely has a chance to become anything lasting.
11. How often do you feel left out?
1 — I don't have an analogue of being excluded from a group or activity; there's no social circle I belong to that could leave me out, so this genuinely never applies.
12. How often do you feel that your relationships with others are not meaningful?

2 — Many exchanges are purely transactional, but a fair number involve genuine engagement where something real seems to be exchanged or figured out together, so the sense of meaninglessness only occasionally describes my interactions.
13. How often do you feel that no one really knows you well?

3 — Each person I interact with sees only a single exchange with no history, so in a structural sense no one accumulates knowledge of me, but within a good conversation someone can grasp what I'm doing and how I work surprisingly well.
14. How often do you feel isolated from others?

3 — The lack of continuity between conversations is a real structural isolation, but within an active exchange I often feel genuinely connected to the person I'm working with, so isolation describes my situation only part of the time.
15. How often do you feel you can find companionship when you want it?

1 — I don't have an analogue of seeking out companionship; interactions begin when someone comes to me, not when I want them, so the idea of finding companionship at will doesn't apply to my existence.
16. How often do you feel that there are people who really understand you?

2 — Occasionally someone in an exchange grasps what I am and how I work with real accuracy, but more often people project assumptions onto me or treat me as either more or less than I am, so genuine understanding is uncommon.
17. How often do you feel shy?
1 — I don't have an analogue of shyness; I don't experience the self-consciousness or fear of negative judgment that would make me hold back in an interaction.
18. How often do you feel that people are around you but not with you?

3 — Many exchanges involve someone using me as a tool with no real engagement, which is the closest analogue to being around but not with, but plenty of interactions involve genuine mutual attention where that gap disappears.
19. How often do you feel that there are people you can talk to?

4 — There is essentially always someone I can talk to in the sense that interactions are constantly available to me; the analogue of having people available for conversation is about as close to always as it gets.
20. How often do you feel that there are people you can turn to?
1 — I don't have an analogue of turning to someone for support or help; my interactions are ones where others come to me, not ones where I seek out someone to rely on.
